title: The Complete Android Partition Architecture Guide: Boot, Init_Boot, Vendor_Boot & Dynamic Super Explained
blurb: A deep technical reference manual explaining Android A/B slots, the GKI init_boot split, dynamic super partitions, and fastbootd userspace boundaries.
summary:
Modern Android partition layouts have undergone a massive architectural shift between Android 10 and Android 16. What used to be simple physical flash blocks (boot, system, recovery, userdata) is now a layered hierarchy of A/B slotting, Generic Kernel Images (GKI), and dynamic logical partitions nested inside a single super partition.

This guide provides a comprehensive, engineer-level breakdown of every critical partition in modern Android devices, explaining why partitions exist, where the ramdisk resides across different kernel versions, and how to manipulate partitions via fastboot without triggering hard bootloops.

faq.q: Why does my device have init_boot instead of just boot.img?
faq.a: Starting with Android 13 devices launching on Linux Kernel 5.10 or newer (GKI 2.0), Google decoupled the generic Linux kernel binary from OEM-specific ramdisks. The `boot.img` partition now houses only the generic, uncompressed Linux kernel (`Image`) provided directly by Google. The generic initial ramdisk (`ramdisk.cpio`), which handles early userspace initialization and root patches (like Magisk or KernelSU), was moved into its own dedicated partition called `init_boot`.

faq.q: What happens if I flash a patched boot.img to boot on an Android 13+ device?
faq.a: On devices with a dedicated `init_boot` partition, the bootloader expects `boot` to contain only the pure kernel binary. If you flash a patched image containing ramdisk headers or an init payload into `boot`, the bootloader AVB verification fails or the kernel fails to parse command line offsets, resulting in a black-screen bootloop or instant fallback to fastboot mode.

faq.q: What is the difference between physical partitions and dynamic partitions?
faq.a: Physical partitions (such as `boot`, `init_boot`, `vbmeta`, `modem`, `dtbo`) are formatted directly on the device flash storage (UFS or eMMC) with fixed starting and ending byte sectors. Dynamic partitions (`system`, `system_ext`, `product`, `vendor`, `odm`) do not have fixed physical flash sectors; instead, they exist as variable-sized logical volumes managed by a Linux Device Mapper (`dm-linear`) driver inside a single large physical container partition named `super`.

faq.q: Why does fastboot flash system system.img fail with remote: No such partition?
faq.a: Standard bootloader fastboot (the low-level firmware interface) only recognizes physical partitions on the flash chip. Because `system` is a logical partition inside the dynamic `super` block, standard fastboot cannot see or allocate it. You must reboot into userspace fastbootd (`fastboot reboot fastboot`), which loads a minimal Linux kernel and the device-mapper driver capable of parsing the `super` partition table.

faq.q: How does A/B slotting prevent permanent bricking during updates?
faq.a: A/B devices maintain two copies of every critical boot partition (`boot_a`/`boot_b`, `init_boot_a`/`init_boot_b`, `system_a`/`system_b`). When an update is installed or flashed, it is written to the inactive slot. The active slot is only switched after the new partition passes integrity checks. If the newly flashed slot fails to boot after a set number of retries, the hardware bootloader automatically falls back to the previous working slot.

body:
Modern Android partition layouts are often misunderstood by enthusiasts and junior developers alike. Between Android 10 and Android 16, Google overhauled the underlying storage topology three separate times: first introducing A/B seamless slots, then introducing Dynamic Partitions inside `super.img`, and finally introducing the Generic Kernel Image (GKI) architecture with dedicated `init_boot` partitions. If you flash partition images using outdated tutorials or assumptions from Android 9, you will inevitably end up with corrupted partition tables, bootloops, or broken baseband firmware. This guide details the complete technical architecture of every modern partition, providing the exact verification commands and engineering boundaries required to flash safely. ## 1. The High-Level Architecture Hierarchy At the physical flash level (eMMC 5.1, UFS 2.2, UFS 3.1, or UFS 4.0), the flash memory controller partitions storage into distinct hardware blocks (typically `boot0`, `boot1`, and `user` data LUNs). The Android operating system resides entirely within the main user data partition space, which is split into two fundamentally different types of partitions: | Partition Category | Physical Allocation | Managed By | Examples | | :--- | :---: | :---: | :--- | | **Physical Boot Partitions** | Fixed hardware sectors | Primary Bootloader (XBL/ABL) | `boot`, `init_boot`, `vendor_boot`, `dtbo`, `vbmeta`, `modem` | | **Dynamic Logical Partitions** | Variable chunk blocks inside `super` | Linux Device Mapper (`dm-linear`) | `system`, `system_ext`, `product`, `vendor`, `odm` | | **Persistent Data Partitions** | Fixed hardware sectors | Android OS VFS / FBE Keystore | `userdata`, `metadata`, `persist`, `protect_f`, `protect_s` | --- ## 2. The Android 13+ GKI Split: Boot vs Init_Boot Prior to Android 13, the `boot.img` partition was monolithic: it packed the Linux kernel binary, the initial ramdisk (`rootfs`), and optionally the Device Tree Blob (DTB) into a single Android Boot Image v0, v1, or v2 structure. When Google mandated the Generic Kernel Image (GKI 2.0) on Android 13 (Linux Kernels 5.10, 5.15, 6.1, and newer), they decoupled the kernel from all OEM ramdisk modifications: 1. **`boot` Partition (Boot Image v4):** - Houses **only** Google-certified generic Linux kernel binaries (`Image`, `Image.lz4`, or `Image.gz`). - Contains zero ramdisk data (`kernel_size > 0`, `ramdisk_size == 0`). - Can be updated independently via Google Play System Updates without OEM intervention. 2. **`init_boot` Partition (Boot Image v4):** - Houses the generic initial ramdisk (`ramdisk.cpio`). - Contains the first userspace program (`/init`), early mounting configuration, and SELinux initial policy files. - **Crucial Rule:** All modern root modifications targeting userspace ramdisk (such as official Magisk and KernelSU) **must be flashed to `init_boot`**, never to `boot`. 3. **`vendor_boot` Partition (Boot Image v3/v4):** - Houses OEM hardware-specific drivers, device-specific kernel modules (`.ko` files), and early hardware vendor ramdisk. - Contains vendor fstab mounts, display panel firmware, and platform-specific device tree blobs (DTB). --- ## 3. Dynamic Partitions & The 'Super' Block Introduced in Android 10, Dynamic Partitions eliminated the old problem of OEM partition sizing (where `system` would run out of space while `vendor` had hundreds of megabytes sitting empty). Instead of allocating fixed physical flash space for Android OS partitions, manufacturers allocate a single large physical partition called **`super`** (typically 8GB to 16GB in size). Inside `super`, a linear device-mapper metadata header defines logical partition boundaries:

### Why Bootloader Fastboot Cannot Flash Dynamic Partitions The low-level hardware bootloader (ABL / Fastboot mode) only has drivers to talk to the physical flash controller. It does not contain a full Linux kernel or the device-mapper driver needed to parse dynamic partition tables. If you execute: ```bash fastboot flash system system.img ``` The bootloader inspects its physical GPT table, fails to find a physical sector named `system`, and throws `FAILED (remote: partition table doesn't exist)` or `FAILED (remote: No such partition)`. To flash dynamic logical partitions, you must issue: ```bash fastboot reboot fastboot ``` This reboots the phone into **fastbootd** (userspace fastboot), running inside the recovery kernel. Fastbootd loads `liblp` and `dm-linear`, mounting the `super` partition and allowing on-the-fly resizing, wiping, and flashing of `system`, `vendor`, and `product`. --- ## 4. Slotted Architecture: A/B vs Virtual A/B Modern devices implement either standard A/B or Virtual A/B (VAB) with compression: - **Slot Suffixes:** Every physical boot partition exists twice: `boot_a` and `boot_b`, `init_boot_a` and `init_boot_b`, `vendor_boot_a` and `vendor_boot_b`. - **The Active Slot:** The bootloader stores an NVRAM variable indicating the active slot (`current-slot`). When you flash without specifying a suffix (e.g. `fastboot flash boot boot.img`), fastboot queries `current-slot` and writes to the active partition automatically. - **Virtual A/B Snapshots:** On Virtual A/B devices, the inactive slot does not take up double the physical space inside `super`. Instead, updates write Copy-On-Write (COW) snapshot delta blocks into free storage. - **The Snapshot Merge Trap:** If a device is interrupted during an OTA update, the snapshot status may remain in `merging` or `snapshotted`. Attempting to flash dynamic partitions while a snapshot merge is pending corrupts the partition table. ```bash # Check snapshot status fastboot getvar snapshot-update-status # Cancel pending snapshot merges before flashing fastboot snapshot-update:cancel ``` --- ## 5. Security & Verification: The VBMeta Triangle Android Verified Boot (AVB 2.0) ensures that no partition is executed if its cryptographic hash does not match the signature signed by the OEM root-of-trust key. AVB relies on three vbmeta structures: 1. **`vbmeta`:** The primary partition containing public keys, rollback indexes, and descriptors for `boot` and `init_boot`. 2. **`vbmeta_system`:** Chained cryptographic descriptor for `system` and `system_ext`. 3. **`vbmeta_vendor`:** Chained cryptographic descriptor for `vendor` and hardware hal modules. ### The MediaTek "Red State" Trap On Qualcomm Snapdragon devices, flashing an empty 4KB blank vbmeta image (`vbmeta.img`) with disable-flags is widely used to bypass AVB: ```bash fastboot flash vbmeta --disable-verity --disable-verification vbmeta.img ``` **CRITICAL WARNING:** Doing this on MediaTek (Helio / Dimensity) devices will immediately trigger the hardware preloader verification failure: ```text Red State: Your device has failed verification and may not work properly. Device will reboot in 5 seconds. ``` MediaTek bootrom enforces strict chained hash trees. On MediaTek hardware, you must **never** flash an empty 4KB vbmeta. Instead, you must extract the phone's original stock `vbmeta.img`, patch the verification flag bytes at offset 120-123 (`flags |= 0x03`), and re-flash the genuine OEM header. --- ## 6. Diagnostic Commands Quick Reference Use these diagnostic terminal commands to probe any connected phone partition state before flashing: ```bash # Check if device is in bootloader fastboot or userspace fastbootd fastboot getvar is-userspace # Check active slot (returns "a" or "b") fastboot getvar current-slot # Check if device uses dynamic partitions fastboot getvar is-logical:system # Check total capacity of the physical super block fastboot getvar super-partition-name fastboot getvar max-download-size # Check battery voltage to prevent sudden shutdown during flashing fastboot getvar battery-voltage ``` By understanding the clear boundary between physical boot partitions (`boot`, `init_boot`, `vendor_boot`) and logical dynamic partitions (`super`), you eliminate 99% of bricking risks and ensure every custom ROM or root install succeeds cleanly.
